Appendix A Derivation of scattering rate formulae

A.1 General formula for dark matter-induced electronic transitions

If a DM particle scatters with an electron in a stationary bound state such as in an atom, it can excite the electron from an initial energy level 1 to an excited energy level 2, by transferring to it energy Δ​E1→2\Delta E_{1\to 2} and momentum q→\vec{q}. The cross section for this process can be derived in a standard way using non-relativistic quantum mechanics, but here we derive it starting from the usual formula for the cross-section in field-theory, in order to make easier connection with the underlying particle physics. We treat the electron as being bound in a static background potential – in other words we approximate the atoms as being infinitely heavy objects which can absorb momentum without recoiling. This is an excellent approximation (<1%<1\% error), since the momentum-transfers we will be interested are typically of order keV.

The cross section for free 2 →\to 2 scattering is given by

σ​vfree=14​Eχ′​Ee′​∫d3​q(2​π)3​d3​k′(2​π)3​14​Eχ​Ee​(2​π)4​δ​(Ei−Ef)​δ3​(k→+q→−k→′)​|ℳfree​(q→)|2¯,\sigma v_{\rm free}=\frac{1}{4E_{\chi}^{\prime}E_{e}^{\prime}}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{d^{3}k^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{1}{4E_{\chi}E_{e}}(2\pi)^{4}\delta(E_{i}-E_{f})\delta^{3}(\vec{k}+\vec{q}-\vec{k}^{\prime})\overline{|\mathcal{M}_{\rm free}(\vec{q}\,)|^{2}}\,, (32)

where ℳfree\mathcal{M}_{\rm free} is the usual field-theory matrix element, and |ℳ|2¯\overline{|\mathcal{M}|^{2}} represents its absolute square averaged over initial spins and summed over final spins.

If the electron were unbound, the non-relativistic scattering amplitude would be given by

⟨χp→−q→,ek→′​|Hint|​χp→,ek→⟩=C​ℳfree​(q→)×(2​π)3​δ3​(k→−q→−k→′),\langle\chi_{\vphantom{\vec{k}}\vec{p}-\vec{q}\,},e_{\vec{k}^{\prime}}|H_{\rm int}|\chi_{\vphantom{\vec{k}}\vec{p}\,},e_{\vec{k}}\rangle=C\,\mathcal{M}_{\rm free}(\vec{q}\,)\times(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}(\vec{k}-\vec{q}-\vec{k}^{\prime})\,, (33)

where |χp→,ek→⟩|\chi_{\vphantom{\vec{k}}\vec{p}\,},e_{\vec{k}}\rangle is plane-wave state for a DM particle of momentum p→\vec{p} and an electron of momentum k→\vec{k}, HintH_{\rm int} is the interaction Hamiltonian, and CC is an unimportant coefficient. However, because the electron is bound it is instead given by

⟨χp→−q→,e2​|Hint|​χp→,e1⟩\displaystyle\langle\chi_{\vphantom{\vec{k}}\vec{p}-\vec{q}\,},e_{2}|H_{\rm int}|\chi_{\vphantom{\vec{k}}\vec{p}\,},e_{1}\rangle =[∫V​d3​k′(2​π)3ψ~2∗(k→′)⟨χp→′,ek→′|]Hint[∫V​d3​k(2​π)3ψ~1(k→)|χp→,ek→⟩]\displaystyle=\bigg[\int\frac{\sqrt{V}d^{3}k^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\widetilde{\psi}_{2}^{*}(\vec{k}^{\prime})\langle\chi_{\vphantom{\vec{k}}\vec{p}\,^{\prime}},e_{\vec{k}^{\prime}}|\bigg]H_{\rm int}\bigg[\int\frac{\sqrt{V}d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\widetilde{\psi}_{1}(\vec{k})|\chi_{\vphantom{\vec{k}}\vec{p}\,},e_{\vec{k}}\rangle\bigg]
=C​ℳfree​(q→)×∫V​d3​k(2​π)3​ψ~2∗​(k→+q→)​ψ~1​(k→),\displaystyle=C\,\mathcal{M}_{\rm free}(\vec{q}\,)\times\!\int\frac{Vd^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\widetilde{\psi}_{2}^{*}(\vec{k}+\vec{q}\,)\widetilde{\psi}_{1}(\vec{k})\,, (34)

where ψ~1\widetilde{\psi}_{1}, ψ~2\widetilde{\psi}_{2} are the (unit normalized) momentum-space wavefunctions of the initial and final electron levels. We have purposefully used plane-wave normalization for both the free and bound electron states: ⟨ek→|ek→⟩=⟨e1|e1⟩=(2​π)3​δ3​(0→)≡V\langle e_{\vec{k}}|e_{\vec{k}}\rangle=\langle e_{1}|e_{1}\rangle=(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}(\vec{0})\equiv V, where VV is the volume of space (which always cancels in the end).

To find the cross section for this excitation process, we can use the free 2 →\to 2 scattering cross section formula but with two replacements: one to account for the modified scattering amplitude, and the other to account for the different final-state phase space. Squaring Eqs. (33, 34), we see that the bound-state scattering amplitude is accounted for by making the replacement

V​(2​π)3​δ3​(k→−q→−k→′)​|ℳfree|2⟶|ℳfree|2×V2​|f1→2​(q→)|2,V(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}(\vec{k}-\vec{q}-\vec{k}^{\prime})|\mathcal{M}_{\rm free}|^{2}\longrightarrow|\mathcal{M}_{\rm free}|^{2}\times V^{2}|f_{1\to 2}(\vec{q}\,)|^{2}\,, (35)

where f1→2​(q→)f_{1\to 2}(\vec{q}\,) is the atomic form factor,

f1→2​(q→)=∫d3​k(2​π)3​ψ~2∗​(k→+q→)​ψ~1​(k→).f_{1\to 2}(\vec{q}\,)=\int\frac{d^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}\widetilde{\psi}_{2}^{*}(\vec{k}+\vec{q}\,)\widetilde{\psi}_{1}(\vec{k})\,. (36)

Fourier transforming Eq. (36) gives the definition given in Eq. (14).

Since there is only one final electron state being considered, we also need to remove the usual final-state phase space integral:

free-electron phase space=V​∫d3​k′(2​π)3⟶1.\text{free-electron phase space}=V\int\frac{d^{3}k^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\longrightarrow 1\,. (37)

Combining Eqs. (32, 35, 37), we can write the formula for the cross-section for a DM particle to excite an electron from level 1 to level 2:

σ​v1→2=14​Eχ′​Ee′​∫d3​q(2​π)3​14​Eχ​Ee​2​π​δ​(Ei−Ef)​|ℳfree​(q→)|2¯×|f1→2​(q→)|2.\sigma v_{1\to 2}=\frac{1}{4E_{\chi}^{\prime}E_{e}^{\prime}}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{1}{4E_{\chi}E_{e}}2\pi\delta(E_{i}-E_{f})\overline{|\mathcal{M}_{\rm free}(\vec{q}\,)|^{2}}\times|f_{1\to 2}(\vec{q}\,)|^{2}\,. (38)

Since we are in the non-relativistic regime, the energies are given by

Ei\displaystyle E_{i} =mχ+me+12​mχ​v2+Ee,1\displaystyle=m_{\chi}+m_{e}+\frac{1}{2}m_{\chi}v^{2}+E_{e,1} (39)
Ef\displaystyle E_{f} =mχ+me+|mχ​v→−q→|22​mχ+Ee,2.\displaystyle=m_{\chi}+m_{e}+\frac{|m_{\chi}\vec{v}-\vec{q}\,|^{2}}{2m_{\chi}}+E_{e,2}\,. (40)

Using the following definitions [9] to parametrize the underlying DM–electron coupling

|ℳfree​(q→)|2¯≡|ℳfree​(α​me)|2¯×|FDM​(q)|2\displaystyle\overline{|\mathcal{M}_{\rm free}(\vec{q}\,)|^{2}}\equiv\overline{|\mathcal{M}_{\rm free}(\alpha m_{e})|^{2}}\times|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2} (41)
σ¯e≡μχ​e2​|ℳfree​(α​me)|2¯16​π​mχ2​me2,\displaystyle\overline{\sigma}_{e}\equiv\frac{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}\overline{|\mathcal{M}_{\rm free}(\alpha m_{e})|^{2}}}{16\pi m_{\chi}^{2}m_{e}^{2}}\,, (42)

the cross section simplifies to

σv1→2=σ¯eμχ​e2∫d3​q4​πδ(ΔE1→2+q22​mχ−qvcosθq​v)×|FDM(q)|2|f1→2(q→)|2.\sigma v_{1\to 2}=\frac{\overline{\sigma}_{e}}{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{4\pi}\,\delta\Big(\Delta E_{1\to 2}+\frac{q^{2}}{2m_{\chi}}-qv\cos\theta_{qv}\Big)\times|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2}|f_{1\to 2}(\vec{q}\,)|^{2}\,. (43)

A.2 Average rate in a dark matter halo

The actual rate of excitation events, for a given transition and a given target electron, is found by multiplying Eq. (43) by the DM density and averaging over the DM velocity distribution gχ​(v→)g_{\chi}(\vec{v}),

R1→2=ρχmχ​∫d3​v​gχ​(v→)​σ​v1→2.R_{1\to 2}=\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\int d^{3}v\,g_{\chi}(\vec{v})\,\sigma v_{1\to 2}\,. (44)

In general, both the electron wavefunctions and the DM velocity distribution will not be spherically symmetric. As noted in [9], the rate will then depend on the orientation of the target with respect to the galaxy. Here we ignore this interesting complication, and approximate the velocity distribution as being spherically symmetric. We can then use the d3​vd^{3}v integral to eliminate the δ\delta-function in Eq. (43), giving

R1→2\displaystyle R_{1\to 2} =ρχ/mχσ¯eμχ​e2∫d3​q4​π∫v2​d​v​d​ϕvq​vgχ(v)Θ(v−vmin(q,ΔE1→2))×|FDM(q)|2|f1→2(q→)|2\displaystyle=\rho_{\chi}/m_{\chi}\frac{\overline{\sigma}_{e}}{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int\frac{d^{3}q}{4\pi}\int\frac{v^{2}dvd\phi_{v}}{qv}\,g_{\chi}(v)\,\Theta\Big(v-v_{\rm min}(q,\Delta E_{1\to 2})\Big)\times|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2}|f_{1\to 2}(\vec{q}\,)|^{2}
=ρχ/mχσ¯e8​π​μχ​e2∫d3q1qη(vmin(q,ΔE1→2))|FDM(q)|2|f1→2(q→)|2.\displaystyle=\rho_{\chi}/m_{\chi}\frac{\overline{\sigma}_{e}}{8\pi\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int d^{3}q\,\frac{1}{q}\eta\big(v_{\rm min}(q,\Delta E_{1\to 2})\big)|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2}|f_{1\to 2}(\vec{q}\,)|^{2}\,. (45)

Here η⁡(vmin)\eta(v_{\rm min}) has its usual definition,

η⁡(vmin)=∫d3​vv​gχ​(v)​Θ​(v−vmin),\eta(v_{\rm min})=\int\frac{d^{3}v}{v}\,g_{\chi}(v)\,\Theta(v-v_{\rm min})\,, (46)

and vminv_{\rm min} is a function of qq and the energy transfer given by

vmin​(q,Δ​E1→2)=Δ​E1→2q+q2​mχ.v_{\rm min}(q,\Delta E_{1\to 2})=\frac{\Delta E_{1\to 2}}{q}+\frac{q}{2m_{\chi}}\,. (47)

A.3 Ionizing an isolated atom

For the purposes of connecting with previous work [9], in this subsection we consider ionization of electrons bound in isolated atomic potentials. We derive the ionization rate of such a system, assuming a spherical atomic potential and filled shells. This approximation was used in [9] to model a liquid xenon target material, and the results below reproduce Eqs. (5) and (6) of that paper. The full calculation of event rates in liquid xenon would require knowledge of electron wavefunctions in the dense, disordered xenon liquid. This is a more challenging calculation than for a semiconductor crystal, but can in principle be performed with similar methods – we leave this for future work. The corrections, however, can be argued to be small, lowering the ionization threshold and increasing the event rate.

An electron ionized from an atom can be treated as being in one of a continuum of positive-energy bound states. These states are affected by the potential well of the atom, but can be approximated as free particle states at asymptotically large radii. We denote their wavefunctions as ψ~k′​l′​m′​(x→)\widetilde{\psi}_{k^{\prime}l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\vec{x}), where l′l^{\prime} and m′m^{\prime} are angular quantum numbers, and k′k^{\prime} is the momentum at asymptotically large radius. The energy of such a state is therefore ER=k′2/2​meE_{R}=k^{\prime 2}/2m_{e}.

The ionization rate for such an atom is found by taking Eq. (45), summing over occupied electron shells, and integrating over the phase space of all possible ionized states. Since these are asymptotically free spherical-wave states, the phase space is

ionized electron phase space=∑l′​m′∫k′2​d​k′(2​π)3=12​∑l′​m′∫k′3​d​ln⁡ER(2​π)3,\text{ionized electron phase space}=\sum_{l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\int\frac{k^{\prime 2}dk^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\int\frac{k^{\prime 3}d\ln E_{R}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,, (48)

when the wavefunction normalization is, as in [9], taken to be

⟨ψ~k′​l′​m′|ψ~k​l​m⟩=(2​π)3​δl′​l​δm′​m​1k2​δ​(k−k′).\langle\widetilde{\psi}_{k^{\prime}l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}|\widetilde{\psi}_{klm}\rangle=(2\pi)^{3}\delta_{l^{\prime}l}\delta_{m^{\prime}m}\frac{1}{k^{2}}\delta(k-k^{\prime})\,. (49)

Plugging this in, the ionization rate is given by

Rion\displaystyle R_{\rm ion} =\displaystyle= ρχmχσ¯e16​π​μχ​e2×\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\overline{\sigma}_{e}}{16\pi\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\times (50)
∑occupiedstates∑l′​m′∫k′3​d​ln⁡ER​d3​q(2​π)3​q​η​(vmin​(q,EB​i+k′2/2​me))​|FDM​(q)|2​|fi→k′​l′​m′​(q→)|2.\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rm occupied\\ \rm states\end{subarray}}\sum_{l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\int\frac{k^{\prime 3}d\ln E_{R}\,d^{3}q}{(2\pi)^{3}q}\,\eta\big(v_{\rm min}(q,E_{Bi}+k^{\prime 2}/2m_{e})\big)|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2}|f_{i\to k^{\prime}l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\vec{q}\,)|^{2}\,.

where EB​iE_{Bi} is the binding energy of occupied state ii.

Since the potential is assumed to be spherically symmetric, and we are ionizing a full atomic shell, we can sum |f1→k′​l′​m′​(q→)|2|f_{1\to k^{\prime}l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\vec{q}\,)|^{2} over initial and final angular momentum variables and the result cannot depend on the direction of q→\vec{q}. This means we can define the dimensionless ionization form factor,

|fion​(k′,q)|2=2​k′3(2​π)3​∑occupiedstates∑l′​m′|∫d3​x​ψ~k′​l′​m′∗​(x→)​ψi​(x→)​ei​q→⋅x→|2.\big|f_{\rm ion}(k^{\prime},q)\big|^{2}=\frac{2k^{\prime 3}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rm occupied\\ \rm states\end{subarray}}\sum_{l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\Big|\int d^{3}x\,\widetilde{\psi}_{k^{\prime}l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}^{*}(\vec{x})\psi_{i}(\vec{x})e^{i\vec{q}\cdot\vec{x}}\Big|^{2}\,. (51)

After applying this definition to the previous equation, we can replace the d3​qd^{3}q integral with 4​π​q2​d​q4\pi q^{2}dq, giving

d​Riond​ln⁡ER=ρχ/mχσ¯e8​μχ​e2∫qdq|FDM(q)|2|fion(k′,q)|2η(vmin(q,EB​i+k′2/2me)).\frac{dR_{\rm ion}}{d\ln E_{R}}=\rho_{\chi}/m_{\chi}\frac{\overline{\sigma}_{e}}{8\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\int qdq\,|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2}\big|f_{\rm ion}(k^{\prime},q)\big|^{2}\eta\big(v_{\rm min}(q,E_{Bi}+k^{\prime 2}/2m_{e})\big)\,. (52)

This reproduces the formulae given in [9].

A.4 Excitations in a semiconductor crystal

In the periodic lattice of a semiconductor crystal, the electron energy levels form a complicated band structure, with an energy gap separating the filled valence bands and the unoccupied conduction bands (Fig. 4). Each possible electron level is labelled by a band index ii and a wavevector k→\vec{k} in the first Brillouin Zone (BZ). Due to the periodicity of the potential, the wavefunctions of these states are in Bloch form,

ψi​k→​(x→)=1V​∑G→ui​(k→+G→)​ei⁡(k→+G→)⋅x→,\psi_{i\vec{k}}(\vec{x})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}\sum_{\vec{G}}u_{i}(\vec{k}+\vec{G})e^{i(\vec{k}+\vec{G})\cdot\vec{x}}\,, (53)

where the G→\vec{G}’s are the reciprocal lattice vectors. Here VV is the volume of the crystal, and the wavefunctions are taken to be unit-normalized, so that

∑G→|ui​(k→+G→)|2=1\displaystyle\sum_{\vec{G}}\big|u_{i}(\vec{k}+\vec{G})\big|^{2}=1 (54)

(We use the relations ∫d3​x​ei​k→⋅x→=(2​π)3​δ3​(k→)\int d^{3}x\,e^{i\vec{k}\cdot\vec{x}}=(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}(\vec{k}) and (2​π)3​δ3​(0→)=V(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}(\vec{0})=V.)

With this form for the wavefunctions, the form factor Eq. (14) to excite from valence level {i​k→}\{i\,\vec{k}\} to conduction level {i′​k→′}\{i^{\prime}\,\vec{k}^{\prime}\} becomes

|fi​k→→i′​k→′​(q→)|2\displaystyle\big|f_{i\vec{k}\to i^{\prime}\vec{k}^{\prime}}(\vec{q})\big|^{2} =|∑G→​G→′(2​π)3​δ3​(k→+q→−k→′−G→′)V​ui′∗​(k→′+G→+G→′)​ui​(k→+G→)|2\displaystyle=\Big|\sum_{\vec{G}\,\vec{G}^{\prime}}\frac{(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}(\vec{k}+\vec{q}-\vec{k}^{\prime}-\vec{G}^{\prime})}{V}u_{i^{\prime}}^{*}(\vec{k}^{\prime}+\vec{G}+\vec{G}^{\prime})u_{i}(\vec{k}+\vec{G})\Big|^{2} (55)
=∑G→′(2​π)3​δ3​(q→−(k→′+G→′−k→))V​|∑G→ui′∗​(k→′+G→+G→′)​ui​(k→+G→)|2.\displaystyle=\sum_{\vec{G}^{\prime}}\frac{(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}\big(\vec{q}-(\vec{k}^{\prime}+\vec{G}^{\prime}-\vec{k})\big)}{V}\Big|\sum_{\vec{G}}u_{i^{\prime}}^{*}(\vec{k}^{\prime}+\vec{G}+\vec{G}^{\prime})u_{i}(\vec{k}+\vec{G})\Big|^{2}\,. (56)

We define the term in the absolute square in Eq. (56) to be f[i​k→,i′​k→′,G→′]f_{[i\vec{k},i^{\prime}\vec{k}^{\prime},\vec{G}^{\prime}]}:

f[i​k→,i′​k→′,G→′]=∑G→ui′∗​(k→′+G→+G→′)​ui​(k→+G→).f_{[i\vec{k},i^{\prime}\vec{k}^{\prime},\vec{G}^{\prime}]}=\sum_{\vec{G}}u_{i^{\prime}}^{*}(\vec{k}^{\prime}+\vec{G}+\vec{G}^{\prime})u_{i}(\vec{k}+\vec{G})\,. (57)

Inserting this into Eq. (45), we can use the δ\delta-function to eliminate the d3​qd^{3}q integral, giving

Ri​k→→i′​k→′=ρχmχ​π2​σ¯eμχ​e2​1V​∑G→′1q​η​(vmin​(q,Ei′​k→′−Ei​k→))​|FDM​(q)|2​|f[i​k→,i′​k→′,G→′]|2|q=|k→′+G→′−k→|.\displaystyle R_{i\vec{k}\to i^{\prime}\vec{k}^{\prime}}=\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{\pi^{2}\overline{\sigma}_{e}}{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\vec{G}^{\prime}}\frac{1}{q}\eta\big(v_{\rm min}(q,E_{i^{\prime}\vec{k}^{\prime}}-E_{i\vec{k}})\big)\,|F_{\rm DM}(q)|^{2}\,\big|f_{[i\vec{k},i^{\prime}\vec{k}^{\prime},\vec{G}^{\prime}]}\big|^{2}\bigg|_{q=|\vec{k}^{\prime}+\vec{G}^{\prime}-\vec{k}|}\,. (58)

The total excitation rate for an electron in level {i​k→}\{i\,\vec{k}\} is found by summing Eq. (58) over all unfilled final energy levels i′i^{\prime},

Ri​k→→any=∑i′∫BZV​d3​k′(2​π)3​Ri​k→→i′​k→′.R_{i\vec{k}\to\rm any}=\sum_{i^{\prime}}\int_{\rm BZ}\frac{Vd^{3}k^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{3}}R_{i\vec{k}\to i^{\prime}\vec{k}^{\prime}}\,. (59)

Note that we do not sum over final electron spins here as that sum has already been included in the definition of σ¯e\overline{\sigma}_{e}.

The total rate of excitation events in the crystal, RcrystalR_{\rm crystal}, is given by summing Eq. (59) over all filled initial levels ii,

Rcrystal=2​∑i∫BZV​d3​k(2​π)3​Ri​k→→any.R_{\rm crystal}=2\sum_{i}\int_{\rm BZ}\frac{Vd^{3}k}{(2\pi)^{3}}R_{i\vec{k}\to\rm any}\,. (60)

Here the extra factor of 2 is the sum over the two degenerate spin states of the filled valence bands.

Putting this together gives the total excitation rate in a crystal,

Rcrystal=ρχmχ​2​π2​σ¯eμχ​e2​V​∑i​i′∫BZd3​k​d3​k′(2​π)6​∑G→′1q​η​(vmin​(q,Ei′​k→′−Ei​k→))​FDM​(q)2​|f[i​k→,i′​k→′,G→′]|2,R_{\rm crystal}=\frac{\rho_{\chi}}{m_{\chi}}\frac{2\pi^{2}\overline{\sigma}_{e}}{\mu_{\chi e}^{2}}V\sum_{i\,i^{\prime}}\!\int_{\rm BZ}\frac{d^{3}k\,d^{3}k^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{6}}\sum_{\vec{G}^{\prime}}\frac{1}{q}\eta\big(v_{\rm min}(q,E_{i^{\prime}\vec{k}^{\prime}}-E_{i\vec{k}})\big)\,F_{\rm DM}(q)^{2}\,\big|f_{[i\vec{k},i^{\prime}\vec{k}^{\prime},\vec{G}^{\prime}]}\big|^{2}\,, (61)

where again q=|k→′+G→′−k→|q=|\vec{k}^{\prime}+\vec{G}^{\prime}-\vec{k}|. Note that this is the total event rate for the whole crystal, and so it is appropriate that it is proportional to the volume VV of the whole crystal. Since the dependence on the DM velocity distribution and interaction type are entirely encoded in η\eta and FDMF_{\rm DM}, which are functions only of the momentum transfer qq and energy deposited EeE_{e}, it is useful to insert delta-functions into the above expression as follows:

For simplicity we assume that the DM velocity distribution, gχ​(v→χ)g_{\chi}(\vec{v}_{\chi}), takes the form of a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution in the galactic rest frame, with a hard cutoff at the galactic escape velocity. In the Earth’s frame the velocity distribution then takes the form

Appendix C Convergence of the Numerical Results

In this section, we investigate the dependence of our calculation on the kinetic-energy cutoff, EcutE_{\rm cut}, (see Eq. (24)) and on the kk-point mesh. The choice of EcutE_{\rm cut} determines the maximum allowed three-momentum transfer qq, which impacts the maximum EeE_{e} that we sample. Truncating the range of qq can have more of an effect for high DM masses and high electron thresholds, since these two regimes depend on high values of qq. On the other hand, the kk-points included in the mesh determine the computationally allowed values of qq. A higher-resolution mesh is particularly important for low EeE_{e} transitions to the bottom of the conduction band, and is therefore especially important for low DM masses and low electron thresholds.

In Fig. 10, we show the dependence of vm​i​nv_{min} in Eq. (16) on qq for different mχm_{\chi} and EeE_{e}. The choice of EcutE_{\rm cut} (top axis) determines the range of qq (bottom axis). In Fig. 11, we show the ratio of the rate for different values of EcutE_{\rm cut} to the rate at Ecut=70E_{\rm cut}=70 Ry for mχ=1m_{\chi}=1 GeV for silicon targets. We see that the error in the rate with our choice of Ecut=70E_{\rm cut}=70 Ry is <𝒪⁡(1%)<{\mathcal{O}}(1\%). The EcutE_{\rm cut} convergence in germanium is slightly worse due to the fact that we are solving for the 3d electrons instead of including them in the pseudopotential. This effect is greatest near the 3d shell energies (a few percent uncertainty), as seen in Fig. 12. In left plots of both Fig. 11 and  12, we see a step-like transition between 30 Ry and the other curves for 11e because 30 Ry is not a high enough energy cutoff to accurately calculate the rate for 11e. The irregular behavior in the distributions on the right side of Fig. 12 are from the semicore electrons in Ge. We do not see the same behavior in Fig. 11, which considers Si and no semicore electrons.

We investigate the effects of our choice of kk-point mesh on our results in two ways.88 8 We do this only for the valence electrons without including the 3d-shell electrons, since energy of the latter are nearly constant as a function of k→\vec{k}. In any case, the 3d-shell electrons are important at large EeE_{e}, while the choice of kk-point mesh is important only at low EeE_{e}. First, we vary the number of kk-points in our mesh and find that there is sensitivity to our choice at low masses and thresholds, see Fig. 13. Second, we perturb each point on the mesh with a random shake of amplitude up to half the lattice-spacing so as to cover the entire kk-space. We use an energy cutoff of Ecut=70E_{\rm cut}=70 Ry and 243 kk-points. The amplitude of our perturbations is Δ​k=0.08\Delta k=0.08 a.u. as the lattice spacing for 243 kk-points is 0.17 a.u. We run 10 independent simulations and plot the results in Fig. 14. We find that our choice of kk-point mesh does not appreciably affect our results for masses above ∼1\sim 1 MeV.

Appendix D The importance of the 3d-shell in germanium

The importance of the 3d-shell electrons in germanium are illustrated in Fig. 15. We see that they dominate the rate at high recoil energies and thus for high thresholds. We discuss this in more detail in §6.2.

Appendix E A Monte Carlo model of secondary scattering

In the main results of this paper, we modeled the ionization response of a target crystal with the linear treatment described in §5. For comparison, here we attempt to mock-up the secondary scattering with a Monte Carlo model, following [101]. The deposited energy EeE_{e} is randomly split between an initial electron and hole. In each following step, each electron or hole with energy above a threshold EionE_{\rm ion} then generates an extra electron-hole pair, with the energy being randomly split between the three particles. This is iterated until all particles have energy less than EionE_{\rm ion}.

The random energy splittings follows a distribution that weights all phase space volume equally, with the density of states assumed to grow as E\sqrt{E} above and below the bandgap, as in a simple 2-band free electron/hole system. Explicitly, for the initial 1→21\to 2 splitting the probability distribution for energy E0E_{0} to split into energies E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} has the form

d​P∝E1​E2​δ​(E0−E1−E2−Egap)​d​E1​d​E2,dP\propto\sqrt{E_{1}}\sqrt{E_{2}}\,\delta(E_{0}-E_{1}-E_{2}-E_{\rm gap})\,dE_{1}\,dE_{2}\,,

while for the subsequent 1→31\to 3 splittings it has the form

d​P∝E1​E2​E3​δ​(E0−E1−E2−E3−Egap)​d​E1​d​E2​d​E3,dP\propto\sqrt{E_{1}}\sqrt{E_{2}}\sqrt{E_{3}}\,\delta(E_{0}-E_{1}-E_{2}-E_{3}-E_{\rm gap})\,dE_{1}\,dE_{2}\,dE_{3}\,,

where electon/hole energies are measured above/below the upper/lower edge of the band gap. We ignore phonon losses during the cascade – these are understood to be quantitatively fairly small, and should not affect the qualitative conclusions.

The output of the Monte Carlo model is a probability distribution P⁡(Q|Ee)P(Q|E_{e}) to get ionization QQ given a deposited energy EeE_{e}. Given the band-gap energy of Egap=0.67E_{\rm gap}=0.67 eV (1.11 eV) in germanium (silicon), we find that Eion=2.67E_{\rm ion}=2.67 eV (3.1 eV) reproduces the measured values of ε\varepsilon for high energy recoils (see Eq. (27)). The distributions for both elements have Fano factors of F≈0.1F\approx 0.1 for all energies above ∼10\sim\!10 eV, consistent with measurements. We illustrate the probability distributions in Fig. 16. In Fig. 17, we show the effect on the event rate of using this model rather than the naive linear model of §5. For thresholds of 2 to 4 electron-hole pairs, downward fluctuations reduce the rate compared to the naive estimate. For higher thresholds, occasional upward fluctuations combined with the steeply falling recoil spectrum lead to an increase in the rate. However, the two models are consistent within a few tens of percent.

Appendix F Review of Density Functional Theory and Pseudopotentials

In this appendix, we review the formalism of density functional theory (DFT), explain in more detail the approximations used in the computation of the wavefunctions, and further explain the numerical methods.

F.1 Electronic structure within DFT

Non-relativistic electrons interacting electrostatically with fixed nuclei are described by the electronic structure Schrödinger equation

[−12​me∑α∇α2−∑α,IZI​e2|r→α−R→I|+∑α<βe2|r→α−r→β|]Ψi(r→1,…,r→N)=εiΨi(r→1,…,r→N),\left[-\frac{1}{2m_{e}}\sum_{\alpha}\nabla_{\alpha}^{2}-\sum_{\alpha,I}\frac{Z_{I}e^{2}}{\left|\vec{r}_{\alpha}-\vec{R}_{I}\right|}+\sum_{\alpha<\beta}\frac{e^{2}}{\left|\vec{r}_{\alpha}-\vec{r}_{\beta}\right|}\right]\Psi_{i}\left(\vec{r}_{1},\dots,\vec{r}_{N}\right)=\varepsilon_{i}\Psi_{i}\left(\vec{r}_{1},\dots,\vec{r}_{N}\right), (70)

where α,β=1,2,⋯,N\alpha,\beta=1,2,\cdots,N label electrons, I=1,2,⋯,MI=1,2,\cdots,M labels nuclei, and ZIZ_{I} is the atomic number of nuclei II. The first term in the Hamiltonian is the electron kinetic energy TT, the second term is the Coulomb electron-nucleus attraction VextV_{\text{ext}} and the third term is the electron-electron Coulomb repulsion Ve​eV_{ee}. The constant nuclei-nuclei term has been omitted. Even though the question is well-posed, obtaining the many-electron wavefunctions Ψi​(r→1,…,r→N)\Psi_{i}\left(\vec{r}_{1},\dots,\vec{r}_{N}\right) computationally is an extremely difficult task because of the exponential scaling of the problem with the number of electrons NN. This method becomes then helpless for applications of interest, so in practice one needs to resort to approximate methods.

DFT is a reformulation of the interacting quantum many-body problem in terms of functionals of the particle density n⁡(𝐫)n(\mathbf{r}). For the case of electrons, the Hohenberg-Kohn theorems [91] imply that all properties of the interacting system are determined once the ground state electron density is known. Minimizing an energy functional E⁡[n]E\left[n\right] will provide the ground state density n0​(𝐫)n_{0}(\mathbf{r}) and the ground state energy E0E_{0}. Unfortunately this energy functional is not known in general. The Kohn-Sham method [92] overcomes this obstacle by replacing the description strictly in terms of functionals for a wavefunction formulation: the system of interacting electrons with Hamiltonian H=T+Ve​e+VextH=T+V_{ee}+V_{\text{ext}} is mapped into a system of independent electrons under the presence of an auxiliary potential H~=T+Va​u​x+Vext\tilde{H}=T+V_{aux}+V_{\text{ext}} which produces the same ground state density as HH. This is of great advantage because, once this mapping is built, one has to solve the much simpler independent-particle system in order to obtain E0E_{0} and n0​(𝐫)n_{0}(\mathbf{r}). However, this comes at the expense of having to use an approximate auxiliary potential VauxV_{\text{aux}}. Typically, VauxV_{\text{aux}} is split into the mean-field Hartree potential VHartree​(r→)=e​∫d3​r→′​n​(r→′)/|r→−r→′|V_{\text{Hartree}}(\vec{r})=e\int d^{3}\vec{r}^{\prime}n(\vec{r}^{\prime})/\left|\vec{r}-\vec{r}^{\prime}\right| and the so-called exchange-correlation potential Vx​cV_{xc}, where the approximations are imposed. Once an approximation for Vx​cV_{xc} has been chosen, the non-interacting electron Schrödinger equation

[−∇22​me+Vext​(r→)+VHartree​(r→)+Vx​c​(r→)]​ψi​(r→)=ϵi​ψi​(r→),\left[-\frac{\nabla^{2}}{2m_{e}}+V_{\text{ext}}(\vec{r})+V_{\text{Hartree}}(\vec{r})+V_{xc}(\vec{r})\right]\psi_{i}(\vec{r})=\epsilon_{i}\psi_{i}(\vec{r}), (71)

which are known as the Kohn-Sham equations, are solved to get the auxiliary Kohn-Sham wavefunctions ψi​(r→)\psi_{i}(\vec{r}). From these, the density can be obtained as n⁡(r→)=∑ifi​|ψi​(r→)|2n(\vec{r})=\sum_{i}f_{i}\left|\psi_{i}(\vec{r})\right|^{2}, where fif_{i} are the occupation numbers (fi=2f_{i}=2 for spin-unpolarized systems) as well as the ground state energy by evaluating the energy density functional99 9 The connection between an energy functional and its corresponding local potential is E⁡[n]=∫d3​r→​n​(r→)​V​(r→)E[n]=\int d^{3}\vec{r}\,n(\vec{r})\,V(\vec{r}). E⁡[n]=T⁡[n]+Eext​[n]+EHartree​[n]+Ex​c​[n]E\left[n\right]=T\left[n\right]+E_{\text{ext}}\left[n\right]+E_{\text{Hartree}}\left[n\right]+E_{xc}\left[n\right],1010 10 The kinetic energy is calculated from the Kohn-Sham wavefunctions as T=1/2me∑i|∇ψi|2T=1/2m_{e}\sum_{i}\left|\nabla\psi_{i}\right|^{2}. as well as a set of wavefunctions ψi\psi_{i} and eigenenergies εi\varepsilon_{i}. This problem is solved self-consistently until convergence is reached.

Expanding the wavefunctions in a finite plane-wave basis with elements labeled by the vectors G→\vec{G} and G→′\vec{G}^{\prime}, the Kohn-Sham equations become the matrix equations

∑G→′HG→,G→′​(k→)​ui​(k→+G→)=Ei​(k→)​ui​(k→+G→).\sum_{\vec{G}^{\prime}}H_{\vec{G},\vec{G}^{\prime}}(\vec{k})u_{i}(\vec{k}+\vec{G})=E_{i}(\vec{k})u_{i}(\vec{k}+\vec{G}). (72)

where the Hamiltonian is

HG→,G→′(k→)=⟨k→+G→|H|k→+G→′⟩=12​me|k→+G→|2δG→,G→′+V(G→−G→′).H_{\vec{G},\vec{G}^{\prime}}(\vec{k})=\left\langle\vec{k}+\vec{G}\right|H\left|\vec{k}+\vec{G}^{\prime}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{2m_{e}}\left|\vec{k}+\vec{G}\right|^{2}\delta_{\vec{G},\vec{G}^{\prime}}+V(\vec{G}-\vec{G}^{\prime})\,. (73)

It should be noted that, since the potential is local, its reciprocal space form does not depend on k→\vec{k}. Furthermore, the Kohn-Sham equations in reciprocal space Eq. (72) decouple different k→\vec{k}’s, so the eigenvalue problem can be carried out independently at each k→\vec{k}.

Despite all the successes of DFT, several notable shortcomings are known today. The most relevant one for us is that DFT is known to give an incorrect band gap. This is due to a discontinuity in the DFT exchange-correlation potential δ​Ex​c/δ​n​(r→)\delta E_{xc}/\delta n(\vec{r}) when electrons are added above the gap [115, 116]. There are methods based on many-body perturbation theory to improve the DFT band gap and band shapes, such as the GW method [117]. However, since the largest contribution to the scattering rate comes from the low energy excitations, we choose to follow an empirical “scissor correction” approach [95, 96]. In this approach a rigid shift is imposed on the conduction bands with respect to the valence bands in order to set the band gap to the experimental values of 1.111.11 eV for silicon and 0.670.67 eV for germanium [97]. It is worth noting that the semiconductor band gap features a temperature variation of around 1010 meV [94], but we are choosing the room temperature band gap values for our calculation.

F.2 Energy Density Functionals

In order to be able to use DFT, a choice for the exchange-correlation functional Ex​c​[n]E_{xc}\left[n\right] is required. The Local Density Approximation (LDA) [92] has been remarkably successful because of its simplicity and transferability. In this method the exchange-correlation energy functional is based only on physical considerations and is approximated locally by the energy of a homogeneous electron gas (HEG) with the following density:

Ex​cLDA​[n]=∫d3​r→​n​(r→)​[ϵxHEG​(n⁡(r→))+ϵcHEG​(n⁡(r→))].E_{xc}^{\text{LDA}}\left[n\right]=\int d^{3}\vec{r}\,n(\vec{r})\,\left[\epsilon_{x}^{\text{HEG}}(n(\vec{r}))+\epsilon_{c}^{\text{HEG}}(n(\vec{r}))\right]. (74)

The HEG exchange [118] and correlation [119] energy functionals are well established. There are some faults in the LDA which are known to be most dramatic where the electrons are highly localized and exchange repulsions are significant. In order to correct for that, the Generalized Gradient Approximations (GGA) introduce a dependence on the density gradient in the exchange-correlation energy density

Ex​cGGA​[n]=∫d3​r→​n​(r→)​ϵx​cGGA​(n⁡(r→),|∇n​(r→)|).E_{xc}^{\text{GGA}}\left[n\right]=\int d^{3}\vec{r}\,n(\vec{r})\,\epsilon_{xc}^{\text{GGA}}(n(\vec{r}),\left|\nabla n(\vec{r})\right|). (75)

In this work we choose the well-established PBE functional [93] which is known to produce a broad set of properties of materials to accuracies of order a few percent [120]. Since LDA functionals tend to underestimate the energies of excited states compared to GGA functionals, we find a difference in cross-section sensitivity of around 10-20%, with a larger difference at higher thresholds.

F.3 Pseudopotentials

The valence electrons are responsible for the formation of interatomic bonds and their wavefunctions are in general delocalized, spanning over interatomic distances. The core electron wavefunctions, however, are very localized around the nucleus and they barely change from the isolated atom to the condensed matter phase. This fact allows to use the atomic core electron wavefunctions in the condensed matter phase by replacing the bare positive nuclear Coulomb potential and the negative Coulomb potential generated by the core wavefunctions with a pseudopotential in the Kohn-Sham problem Eq. (71). The advantage is two-fold: first, the number of electrons in the problem is reduced to the number of valence electrons and second, the only wavefunctions to be calculated are valence wavefunctions which, since they are rather smooth, do not require as fine a grid to represent them as a core electron wavefunction would, thus improving the computational efficiency. In this work we use Vanderbilt-type ultrasoft pseudopotentials [94]. The pseudopotential for Si includes the 3s and 3p electrons in the valence, while in the case of germanium, we use a pseudopotential which includes the 3d, 4s and 4p electrons in the valence.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
